lesson.text: Quick memory: which of the three Rs is best? (Reduce.) Caring for nature is one responsibility. Today: jobs and responsibilities.
A responsibility is a job or a duty that people trust you to do. At home you might feed a pet, lay the table or tidy your room. Others count on you.
In Japan, children take turns to clean their classrooms and to serve school lunch to their class. Everyone helps, so the whole class shares the work.
Class jobs: watering plants, handing out books, tidying up, or being a buddy to a new child. Doing your job well helps everyone.
Being reliable means doing your job without being reminded. A pet cannot feed itself: it depends on you.
A promise is saying you will do something. Only promise what you can really do, and then keep it! If you cannot, tell the person early and explain.
Rights and responsibilities go together: you have the right to learn, and the responsibility to let others learn too.
Try it in the world: look after a buddy or a farm animal in your world. Feed it and keep its home tidy. What promise could you make to it?

choices: a job people trust you to do
exercises.explain: A responsibility is a job or duty that others trust you to do.

exercises.prompt: Which is a responsibility at home?
exercises.hint: Which one is a job that someone counts on?
exercises.explain: Feeding the pet is a job the pet and your family count on you to do.

exercises.prompt: A promise is saying you will do something.
exercises.explain: True: a promise is your word that you will do something.

exercises.prompt: In Japan, many children help to clean their classrooms.
exercises.hint: Remember the lesson card about Japan.
exercises.explain: True: pupils take turns to clean the classroom and serve lunch.

exercises.hint: Think of doing a job without being reminded.
exercises.explain: Reliable means people can count on you to do your job.

exercises.prompt: Why should you only promise what you can really do?
exercises.hint: What happens to trust when a promise is broken?
choices: so you can keep your promise
so you never have to help
exercises.explain: Promising only what you can do means you can keep your word, and people trust you.

exercises.prompt: A pet can look after itself, so feeding it is not a responsibility.
exercises.hint: Can a pet open its own food?
exercises.explain: False: a pet depends on the people who look after it.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for watering the class plants in order.
exercises.explain: Check the soil, fill the can, water each plant, then put the can away.

exercises.prompt: Mimi promised to help Tilly on Saturday but now she is ill. What should she do?
exercises.hint: Remember what to do if you cannot keep a promise.
exercises.explain: Telling Tilly early lets her find other help, and she will still trust Mimi.

exercises.prompt: You have the right to learn. What responsibility goes with it?
choices: to learn only what you like
exercises.explain: Everyone has the right to learn, so your responsibility is to let others learn too.

exercises.prompt: Why do children share the cleaning in many Japanese schools?
exercises.hint: Think about what sharing a job teaches.
choices: so everyone helps and cares for the school
exercises.explain: When everyone helps, the whole class learns to care for its school and each other.

exercises.prompt: If everyone does their class job, the class works better for everyone.
exercises.hint: What happens if nobody waters the plants?
exercises.explain: True: when everyone does their part, the whole class benefits. If the plant waterer forgets, the plants wilt; if the book helper forgets, nobody can start.

exercises.prompt: Bram was asked to feed the chickens. Which shows he is reliable?
exercises.hint: Reliable means others can count on you.
choices: he feeds them without being reminded
he feeds them when he feels like it
he asks Mimi to do it every time
exercises.explain: Feeding them without being reminded shows the chickens and his friends can count on him.

exercises.prompt: Sort these jobs: at home, or in class?
exercises.hint: Where would each job be done?
exercises.explain: At home: feed the pet, lay the table. In class: water the plants, hand out books.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to what it means.
matches: a job people trust you to do
exercises.hint: Reliable people do not need reminding.
exercises.explain: A responsibility is a job people trust you to do, reliable means doing it without reminders, and a promise says you will do something.

exercises.prompt: Mimi feeds her rabbit twice a day. How many times is that in a week?
exercises.hint: A week has 7 days, and each day has 2 feeds.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: a right, or the responsibility that goes with it?
exercises.hint: A right is what you get. A responsibility is what you do for others.
exercises.explain: Rights: to learn, to be listened to, to play. Responsibilities: let others learn, listen to others, and share the toys so others can play too.

exercises.prompt: Bram feeds the chickens 2 times a day. Each time they eat 3 scoops. How many scoops does he need for a week?
exercises.hint: Find the scoops for one day first, then for 7 days.
exercises.explain: Each day: 2 × 3 = 6 scoops. A week has 7 days: 6 × 7 = 42 scoops.
